title: Northstar x Redwood - Security review: Optimize quality gates + audit trail
topics: How Optimize recommendations are applied (one-click vs auto-apply)
Quality gating: offline evals, thresholds, variance, smoke vs full gates
Audit logs: what is recorded, retention, and export/SIEM
Rollout coupling: canary promotion blocks and auto-rollback hooks
Data handling during evals (prompt sets, customer data, artifacts)
summary: Northstar requested a security/controls deep dive focused on Redwood Optimize making cost-saving config changes (batching/caching/quantization) and how Redwood prevents silent quality regressions. Redwood walked through the “quality gate” enforcement model: proposed config diffs trigger static validation + eval-harness runs (smoke gate then full gate) against a baseline; only passing results can be applied. Overrides are time-bound, require an authorized approver, and emit audit log events. Rollout controller blocks canary promotion when gates fail and can auto-rollback if online quality signals degrade. Northstar asked about audit log contents, export to SIEM, RBAC, and whether customer prompts are stored; Redwood described artifact pointers, configurable retention, and enterprise log export options. Next steps: Redwood to share audit event schema/examples, SOC2 package, and a short written description of the override policy and roles; Northstar to confirm internal approver group and desired log retention/export path.
action_items: Redwood (Kevin Osei) to send sample audit log events for: gate_started, gate_completed(pass/fail), override_requested, override_granted, apply_blocked, rollback_triggered.
Redwood (Marcus Lin) to share SOC 2 report + security overview and confirm SSO/SAML + RBAC role mapping for Optimize approvals.
Redwood (Aditya Rao) to send a 1-pager describing gate tiers (smoke vs full), default thresholds, and what changes require full gates (quant profile, risky cache settings).
Northstar (Priya Shah) to confirm whether SIEM ingestion prefers Splunk HEC vs S3 export and desired retention requirements for audit events.
Northstar (Tom Reynolds) to provide a list of routes/models intended for initial Optimize rollout and whether auto-apply is in scope or one-click only.
next_steps: Schedule a 30-min follow-up with Northstar security + platform to review audit event examples and finalize approver/RBAC setup.
Redwood to provision a sandbox account with Optimize gating enabled so Northstar can test a blocked apply + override workflow end-to-end.
Northstar to align internally on whether overrides can be approved by oncall vs security-only, and acceptable max override duration.
transcript:
Meeting: Northstar x Redwood - Security review: Optimize quality gates + audit trail
Recorded: 2026-02-06 17:02 UTC
Duration: 53 minutes
Attendees (Redwood): Marcus Lin, Aditya Rao, Dylan Brooks, Kevin Osei
Attendees (Northstar): Priya Shah, Tom Reynolds, Elena Petrova, James Wu

---

[00:00] Marcus Lin: Alright, we’re recording. Thanks everyone for joining. This is Marcus, I run security reviews on Redwood’s side. The goal today is to go deep on controls around Optimize, especially the quality gates and audit trail, and answer whatever security and governance questions you have.

[00:14] Priya Shah: Yep, thanks Marcus. For context, our concern is less “can you run the model” and more “you’re going to change how it runs.” Like batching, caching, quantization. We need to know how that’s controlled and how we can prove what changed.

[00:29] Aditya Rao: Totally. I’m Aditya, PM for Optimize. We heard similar concerns from other customers—cost savings are great but not at the expense of correctness. So we put mandatory quality evaluation gates in front of any optimization change.

[00:41] Tom Reynolds: And those changes can be automatic, right? Like auto-apply?

[00:45] Aditya Rao: There are two modes. One-click apply in the Console, and auto-apply policies for certain accounts/routes. But both go through the same gating pipeline. There isn’t a backdoor where an automatic change bypasses gates.

[00:58] James Wu: When you say “gating pipeline,” can you walk it end-to-end? Like what happens if Optimize suggests, say, a new quant profile.

[01:06] Aditya Rao: Yep. High-level flow is: Optimize generates a recommendation as a config diff—so literally “before” and “after” values for the runtime knobs. Before we run anything expensive, we do static validation. That catches unsupported combinations, things we know are unsafe (for example, a quant profile not compatible with that model family or GPU SKU), or a cache setting that violates constraints.

[01:29] Dylan Brooks: And just to anchor: we treat the config diff as a typed object, not free-form. That helps with validation and audit.

[01:36] Aditya Rao: After validation, we create a “gate run” record with state: pending → running → passed/failed, and there’s also overridden. Then we trigger eval-harness with two things: the baseline config (current production or pinned baseline), and the proposed config. Eval-harness runs prompt sets and computes metric deltas.

[01:58] Priya Shah: Baseline is what’s live right now on that route?

[02:01] Aditya Rao: Usually yes. For quantization there’s nuance because baseline can depend on hardware—like A100 vs H100, or different kernel path. In those cases we select baseline per model family plus hardware SKU. But it’s explicit and recorded in the gate run.

[02:18] Priya Shah: And the gate says pass/fail based on… what exactly. Accuracy? Rubric score? I’m trying to see if it’s deterministic.

[02:28] Aditya Rao: It’s a set of metrics, and it’s tiered. We have a fast “smoke” gate intended to finish quickly, and a full gate for riskier changes. Metrics include task success / acceptance checks for prompt sets, rubric-based scoring where relevant, and a few model-specific heuristics. We handle variance—minimum sample sizes, confidence bounds, and flake detection. Selene and Jonas on our evals team own the methodology; we can share the v1 thresholds document.

[02:56] Tom Reynolds: How long do these take? Because if it blocks, like, a rollout pipeline, that’s a concern.

[03:02] Dylan Brooks: Smoke gates are designed to be minutes. Full gates can be longer—think tens of minutes depending on suite size and hardware availability. We also have queueing and retry rules, and we emit “gate execution latency” metrics because we don’t want this to become a bottleneck.

[03:21] Priya Shah: Okay. Now the control question: what prevents someone from applying anyway even if it fails? Or like the UI “apply” button.

[03:30] Aditya Rao: The enforcement is defense-in-depth. The Console blocks apply based on gate status, but more importantly the Optimize service enforces at the API boundary. So even if you tried to call the apply endpoint directly, it checks gate state. Failed or missing gates return explicit “blocked” with reasons.

[03:48] Marcus Lin: And for deployments using our rollout controller, canary promotion is also blocked if the associated gate run is failed or absent. So we have both “can’t apply the config change” and “can’t promote the rollout.”

[04:02] James Wu: You mentioned overrides. So there is a mechanism to override failed gates.

[04:07] Marcus Lin: Yes. It’s intentionally structured and time-bound. Override is not “ignore forever.” It requires a user with an approver role, it’s recorded, it includes a reason field, and it has an expiration. After expiration, you can’t keep using override to push further changes without renewing, and renewals are also logged.

[04:29] Priya Shah: Approver role—on your side or our side? We’d want our security team to be the only approvers.

[04:35] Marcus Lin: For hosted, we support customer-controlled RBAC in the Console. So you can decide who in your org can request and who can approve. Redwood can optionally have break-glass admin for support, but that is audited and typically restricted contractually. We also support SSO/SAML so the identities are your identities.

[04:56] Elena Petrova: Sorry to jump in. For procurement, we care about audit and reporting. Can we export audit logs to our SIEM? And what is retained?

[05:05] Kevin Osei: Yep, Kevin here—log export. We generate audit events for gate lifecycle and for configuration changes. At minimum: gate_run_created, eval_triggered, gate_passed, gate_failed, apply_attempted, apply_blocked, apply_succeeded. For overrides: override_requested, override_granted, override_denied, override_expired. Each event includes actor identity, timestamps, route/model identifiers, config diff id, and pointers to artifacts.

[05:34] Elena Petrova: Pointers meaning links to…?

[05:37] Kevin Osei: Links or artifact IDs depending on your plan and region. We avoid embedding large evaluation artifacts into the audit stream. Audit stream is immutable event record; artifacts live in our artifact store with retention controls.

[05:54] Priya Shah: Do the artifacts contain customer prompts? That’s a big one for us.

[06:00] Aditya Rao: Good question. There are two categories. One is our curated gating prompt sets that are not your production prompts. Those are used for the offline gate. Those artifacts are mostly scores, diffs, and some sample outputs. The other is online canary signals—we don’t store raw customer prompts for that by default; it’s aggregated metrics (error rates, latency, some quality proxies if enabled). If you opt into more detailed logging, that’s controlled and documented.

[06:26] Tom Reynolds: So if the gate runs use your prompt sets, how do we know it’s relevant to our domain?

[06:31] Aditya Rao: For general gating, it’s meant to catch broad regressions (formatting, instruction following, long context behavior, etc). For customers with specific requirements, we can incorporate customer-provided prompt sets into the eval harness under a separate agreement. Some customers provide redacted or synthetic prompts. But the MVP is our maintained prompt sets plus online canary coupling.

[06:57] Priya Shah: Okay. Let’s talk about what exactly is changed. Batching and caching—those can change semantics, right?

[07:04] Dylan Brooks: Most batching changes should not change semantics, but in practice it can if it affects truncation policy, timeouts, or streaming behavior. Same with caching—prefix cache and KV cache can surface weirdness if the cache keying is wrong or if there’s a bug. And quantization definitely can change outputs. That’s why we gate all three.

[07:26] Priya Shah: KV cache—sorry the transcript will say “Kiev cache,” but yeah.

[07:30] (crosstalk)

[07:31] Aditya Rao: Right. And because some knobs are riskier, we decide whether smoke gate is enough or full gate is required. Quant profile changes basically always require full gate. Some cache changes, like enabling a new prefix cache strategy, also require full gate.

[07:50] James Wu: Is that policy configurable per route? Like our internal tooling routes are less sensitive than customer-facing.

[07:57] Aditya Rao: Yes. Policy is configurable per route and per tier. So you can say: for Route A, only allow one-click apply with full gates. For Route B, allow auto-apply if smoke gates pass and online canary signals are green. Those policies are also audited.

[08:18] Priya Shah: Where is this policy enforced? In the UI or server-side.

[08:22] Dylan Brooks: Server-side. UI reflects it, but it’s enforced by the Optimize service and the rollout controller. We treat UI as informational.

[08:32] Marcus Lin: And we have an internal architecture decision record that spells out “gates required” and why we didn’t choose monitor-only. I can share the gist; the main point was preventing silent regressions and ensuring traceability.

[08:48] Priya Shah: Great. Let’s drill into the audit log fields. We need actor, what changed, why, and evidence. What do you log as “why”?

[08:57] Kevin Osei: We log “reason codes” where possible. Example: recommendation_reason = “cost_per_token_high” or “gpu_utilization_low” or “batching_opportunity_detected.” For overrides, we require free-text justification, and optionally a structured reason code like “incident_mitigation” or “customer_request” or “false_positive_gate.”

[09:20] Priya Shah: Who can view these logs? We have least-privilege.

[09:24] Marcus Lin: RBAC: you can restrict audit views to specific roles. There’s a separation between “can apply Optimize changes” and “can approve overrides” and “can view audit log export settings.” We can map these to your SSO groups.

[09:42] Tom Reynolds: And what about Redwood staff access? You said break-glass.

[09:46] Marcus Lin: Standard is Redwood support cannot approve overrides for your org. If we ever need to access for debugging, it’s through a privileged access path, time-bound, and audited. We can include that in the security addendum if needed.

[10:05] Elena Petrova: Do you support data residency? We have EU workloads.

[10:09] Marcus Lin: Yes. For hosted, we have regions and we can keep processing and logs in-region depending on configuration. There have been known issues with gate runtime in some regions when GPU capacity is tight; we’ve added retries and region-aware scheduling. If you’re EU-heavy, we can talk about ensuring eval capacity there or running evals in a dedicated project.

[10:35] Priya Shah: So, you run evals on GPUs. That means our config change is evaluated using hardware. Do you pin the hardware?

[10:43] Aditya Rao: For hosted, it’s pinned to the target runtime environment for that route when possible. For quantization in particular we match GPU SKU; if the route runs on H100, we don’t evaluate on an A10 and pretend it’s the same. Baseline selection is per model family + hardware.

[11:03] James Wu: What about retrying evals? If it fails once, do you just fail the gate.

[11:08] Aditya Rao: We have a rerun policy for flaky suites. Eval-harness reports a flake score. If flake is detected, we can rerun and aggregate results, or quarantine a prompt set. But we also don’t want reruns to become a way to “game” it. So there are caps and all attempts are recorded.

[11:32] Priya Shah: Quarantine prompt set—meaning you disable it temporarily?

[11:36] Dylan Brooks: Yep, disable from gating while it’s investigated. That itself is an admin action with an audit event, and it’s not something your end users can do unless you give them that admin role.

[11:52] Priya Shah: Okay. Let’s talk about online canary signals. You said gates are offline evals plus online signals.

[12:00] Aditya Rao: For rollout coupling, offline gates are mandatory before you can even start a canary for an optimization change (depending on policy). Once canary starts, we watch online metrics: error rate, latency, and optionally quality proxies like format adherence, tool-call validity, refusal rate changes, or customer-defined sentinel checks if integrated.

[12:22] Tom Reynolds: Do you have auto-rollback?

[12:24] Aditya Rao: Yes. Rollout controller can halt promotion and rollback if the canary violates thresholds. It’s configurable. And those decisions—halted, rolled back—are also audited.

[12:39] Priya Shah: Good. Now, what if someone does a manual config change outside Optimize? Like via API or some admin panel.

[12:46] Dylan Brooks: If it’s through Redwood control-plane APIs, it’s still logged as a config change. We’re adding “where possible” gating for manual changes too, but at minimum it’s logged and can be required by policy for certain environments.

[13:02] Marcus Lin: In other words, you’ll have an audit record of manual changes even if someone bypasses Optimize recommendations.

[13:09] Priya Shah: “Even if someone bypasses” is scary. Is bypass possible today?

[13:14] Dylan Brooks: For hosted customer-managed routes, changes go through controlled APIs. There’s not like SSH into a box. But some legacy workflows existed where support could tweak settings for incidents; we’re formalizing that into the same audit and approval path.

[13:31] Priya Shah: Okay, thanks for being candid. What’s the retention on audit logs.

[13:36] Kevin Osei: Default retention is plan-based. For enterprise, we can do longer retention and/or export. Export options: streaming to your SIEM (Splunk, Datadog), or periodic delivery to your S3/GCS bucket. We can also provide an API to fetch audit events with pagination.

[13:58] Elena Petrova: We prefer Splunk HEC but S3 is also fine.

[14:01] Kevin Osei: Great. We can follow up on what you prefer. The important piece: audit events are immutable. We don’t allow edits; if something changes (like an override is revoked), that’s a new event.

[14:16] James Wu: Can you show how an override works in practice? Like what steps.

[14:22] Aditya Rao: Sure, I’ll describe it. Say an optimization fails full gate by a small margin. A user hits “Request override” in Console, enters reason, optionally attaches a ticket link. That creates override_requested. An approver gets a notification. Approver reviews the gate results and artifacts, and either denies or grants with an expiration (e.g., 7 days) and scope (route/model). When granted, override_granted event is emitted. Then apply endpoint allows the change *only within that scope* and we still recommend canary rollout.

[14:56] Priya Shah: Can you require two-person approval? Like maker-checker.

[15:01] Marcus Lin: Today it’s one approver role, but we can enforce separation of duties in practice by ensuring the requester cannot be an approver. Two explicit approvals is not in the MVP, but we’ve had requests. We can capture that as a requirement and talk roadmap.

[15:20] Tom Reynolds: For us, it might be enough to ensure approver is a security group. But it depends.

[15:25] Priya Shah: Yeah. Another thing: how do you ensure overrides don’t become permanent. You said expiration.

[15:32] Marcus Lin: Overrides are time-bound. After expiration, if the config is still in place, you’ll see override_expired event and the system can either require re-approval to keep it, or force a revert depending on policy. Typically we do “block further changes without re-approval,” and we recommend reverting if it was a temporary incident workaround.

[15:56] Priya Shah: That’s helpful. Now, about the “quality metrics.” We need to understand if it’s subjective. Rubric scoring means an LLM judge sometimes.

[16:06] Aditya Rao: Yes, some suites use LLM-as-judge. That’s why we incorporate variance modeling and require minimum sample sizes. We also combine with deterministic checks where possible—format compliance, exact match on known answers, tool call schema validity, etc. And we treat flakiness as first-class: we track it and quarantine.

[16:32] Priya Shah: If the judge model changes, does that change gates. Is that tracked?

[16:37] Aditya Rao: Yep. Eval-harness version is recorded, including judge model version. Changing eval harness or thresholds is itself a change with its own change management. We can provide release notes for that.

[16:52] Marcus Lin: From a security perspective, we treat eval policy as “control plane configuration,” so changes are audited internally and can be reported.

[17:02] Elena Petrova: Do you have SOC 2 and ISO.

[17:05] Marcus Lin: SOC 2 Type II, yes. ISO is in progress for later this year. We can share the SOC report under NDA.

[17:16] Tom Reynolds: Let’s get back to the earlier thing—capacity in EU. We saw a support note about timeouts. Is that resolved?

[17:24] Dylan Brooks: There was an issue where gate runs in eu-west could timeout due to GPU scarcity. We added queue awareness, retries, and a guardrail where gates fail “inconclusive” rather than “pass” if they don’t complete. That prevents an optimization from being applied without evidence. Also we have alerts on gate execution latency so SRE sees it.

[17:50] Priya Shah: Inconclusive should block apply.

[17:52] Dylan Brooks: Correct.

[17:55] James Wu: How do you ensure a cost optimization doesn’t change PII handling. Like caching and data retention.

[18:03] Marcus Lin: Great question. Caching settings are constrained by policy. We have modes where caches are in-memory only and not persisted. Any change that would affect retention or persistence is not something Optimize will recommend without explicit configuration, and it’s subject to full gate plus additional compliance checks. Also, cache keys and tenant isolation are part of the runtime safety model.

[18:31] Priya Shah: Are cache contents encrypted.

[18:34] Marcus Lin: For in-memory caches on GPUs/hosts, it’s process memory; at rest encryption applies to persisted artifacts/logs. For anything persisted, yes, encrypted at rest with KMS. Network encryption in transit as well.

[18:52] Tom Reynolds: Okay. Another governance item: can we get a report of “all Optimize changes applied in the last 90 days” with who approved.

[19:01] Kevin Osei: Yes. The audit event API supports filtering by time, route, model, and event type. Console also has an audit view that you can export. If you export to your SIEM, you can run those queries there too.

[19:20] Elena Petrova: And pricing for audit log export is…?

[19:23] Marcus Lin: We can handle that offline with your AE, but generally audit export is included in enterprise tiers; longer retention or higher volume may be an add-on.

[19:34] Priya Shah: I want to ask a “failure mode” question. If Optimize suggests a change and the gate passes, but later we detect regression in prod—what happens.

[19:46] Aditya Rao: Two things. First, rollout controller can auto-rollback on canary if metrics degrade. Second, even post-rollout, we have monitoring and you can pin configs. And we can use those incidents to update prompt sets/thresholds. Importantly, the audit trail lets you tie the regression to a specific config diff and gate run.

[20:12] James Wu: Do you do A/B testing.

[20:14] Aditya Rao: For some customers, yes—A/B or canary. For gating project, we’re focused on canary and promotion blocks, but A/B is supported in Rollouts.

[20:28] Tom Reynolds: You keep saying “config diff.” Is it human-readable?

[20:32] Dylan Brooks: It’s human-readable and machine-readable. Example keys: batching.max_batch_tokens, batching.max_concurrent_requests, cache.prefix_cache.enabled, cache.kv_cache.policy, quant.profile_id. The diff shows old/new and the scope.

[20:55] Priya Shah: Is that diff stored in the audit event or referenced.

[20:59] Kevin Osei: Audit event includes a diff ID and a summarized representation (like “batching policy updated”). Full diff is retrievable via the config API with appropriate permissions.

[21:14] Priya Shah: Can someone delete a config diff.

[21:16] Dylan Brooks: No. You can supersede with a new config version, but you can’t erase history.

[21:23] Priya Shah: Good.

[21:25] Marcus Lin: Can we pause and do a quick recap of what we covered, just to make sure we’re answering your core concerns?

[21:31] Priya Shah: Sure.

[21:32] Marcus Lin: Controls: optimize recommendations are never applied without passing gates (or explicit override). Enforcement is server-side; rollout controller blocks promotion. Audit: immutable events for gate lifecycle, apply attempts, overrides, rollback/halt. RBAC: customer-controlled roles with SSO. Data: offline gating uses Redwood prompt sets by default; online signals are aggregated. Export: SIEM/S3 options. Does that capture it?

[21:58] Priya Shah: Mostly yes. I have a couple more: can you show evidence that a gate ran. Like an artifact we can reference in an audit.

[22:07] Aditya Rao: Yes. Each gate run has an ID. It links to eval-harness run IDs, the suite versions, and the score report. You can click from Console or fetch via API. And those IDs show up in audit events.

[22:26] Priya Shah: And if we do an override, does it still show the failed metric.

[22:30] Aditya Rao: Yes. Override doesn’t hide failure. It’s “failed gate + override granted.” The UI shows that clearly and audit has both.

[22:42] Tom Reynolds: Do you support notifications to Slack or email when a gate fails.

[22:47] Dylan Brooks: Yes—alerts and notifications are part of the observability standard. You can configure webhooks for gate failures or flake spikes.

[22:58] James Wu: Competitor question—Bedrock has guardrails but not this exact thing. I like this gating approach. But what about OpenAI, they don’t allow these knobs.

[23:08] Aditya Rao: Right, the reason this exists is because we *do* allow these cost/perf knobs. So we needed guardrails appropriate for that power.

[23:20] Elena Petrova: Okay. So what do you need from us to proceed.

[23:24] Marcus Lin: Mainly: confirm approver group, decide on export path (Splunk vs S3), and whether you want one-click only initially. Then we can provide the documentation pack: SOC2, audit event examples, and the gating 1-pager.

[23:42] Priya Shah: I’d like the audit event examples soon, like today if possible, or early next week.

[23:47] Kevin Osei: I can send a sample payload set after the call. It’ll be representative, redacted. Just note the exact field names might differ slightly depending on version.

[24:00] Priya Shah: That’s fine.

[24:02] Tom Reynolds: Also, can we get a sandbox where we can intentionally make a change fail.

[24:07] Dylan Brooks: Yes. We can set up a route in a sandbox project and propose a quant profile that we know will degrade, so you can see the fail path, the block, and the override flow.

[24:22] Priya Shah: Perfect.

[24:25] (brief pause)

[24:26] Marcus Lin: Any other questions on security controls before we wrap?

[24:31] Priya Shah: One last: do you have a concept of “break glass” for our own org—like oncall can approve in an incident, but it must be time-bound.

[24:40] Marcus Lin: Yes. You can designate an “Override Approver” group that includes oncall, and set max duration for overrides. We recommend also requiring a ticket link. Again, all of it is logged.

[24:56] Elena Petrova: Okay.

[24:58] James Wu: I’m good.

[25:00] Marcus Lin: Great. Next steps: Kevin sends audit event samples. I’ll send SOC2 and security overview. Aditya sends the gating tiers/thresholds 1-pager. And we’ll schedule a follow-up to confirm RBAC and export. Sound good?

[25:14] Priya Shah: Sounds good.

[25:15] Tom Reynolds: Thanks everyone.

[25:17] Marcus Lin: Thanks.

---
Note: Fireflies transcription had minor term confusion (e.g., “KV cache” occasionally rendered as “Kiev cache”; “eval-harness” as “evil harness” once).
